slides.title: Why do we care about quadratics…

transcription.tex: Quadratic relationships arise in many practical situations.

\textbf{Summations}\[1+2+\cdots+n=\frac12n^2+\frac12n\]A sports event awards 8 points, then 7, then 6, and so on. For \(1\le n\le8\) competitors:\[8+7+\cdots+(9-n)=\frac{n(17-n)}2\]The totals for one, two and three competitors are 8, 15 and 21.

\textbf{Projectile motion}\par Under constant acceleration,\[s=ut+\frac12at^2\]Here \(s\) is displacement, \(u\) initial velocity, \(a\) acceleration and \(t\) time. The expression is quadratic in \(t\).\par A projectile moving under gravity alone follows a parabolic path.

transcription.tex: A function gives a rule that assigns one output to each permitted input. It is a formal version of a number machine.\[\text{input }x\quad\longrightarrow\quad f\quad\longrightarrow\quad\text{output }f(x)\]
\textbf{Example}\quad The function doubles its input. Write its rule.
\[f(x)=2x\]\(f\) is the name of the function; \(f(x)\) is its output for input \(x\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: For \(f(x)=x^2\), example inputs and outputs are:\[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}x&-1&0&1.7&2&3.1\\\hline f(x)&1&0&2.89&4&9.61\end{array}\]
\textbf{Domain and range}\quad What do these terms mean?
The domain is the set of permitted inputs. The range is the set of outputs achieved.\par With domain \(x\in\mathbb R\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) has range \(f(x)\ge0\).
\textbf{Roots}\quad What is a root (or zero) of a function?
A value of \(x\) for which \(f(x)=0\).\par For \(f(x)=x^2\), the only root is \(x=0\).
\(x\in\mathbb R\) reads: \(x\) is a member of the set of real numbers.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Sketching a quadratic}\par Find and label the key features. A sketch does not require a uniform numerical scale.
\textbf{1. Roots}\par Solve \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) to find any \(x\)-intercepts.\par \textbf{2. Vertical intercept}\par Put \(x=0\): the point is \((0,c)\).

transcription.tex: Sketch the graph of \(y={x}^{2}+3x-4\) and find the coordinates of the turning point.
Put \(x=0\). Then \(y=0^2+3(0)-4=-4\), so the graph crosses the vertical axis at \((0,-4)\).
Complete the square.\[y=(x+\tfrac32)^2-\tfrac94-4\]\[=(x+\tfrac32)^2-\tfrac{25}4.\]The square is smallest when \(x=-\tfrac32\). The minimum point is \((-\tfrac32,-\tfrac{25}4)\).

transcription.tex: Determine the equation of this quadratic graph, in the form \(y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c\).
The graph crosses the horizontal axis at \(-3\) and \(2\). Try \(y=(x+3)(x-2)\). The positive leading coefficient gives the correct upward opening.
Expanding gives \(y=x^2+x-6\). At \(x=0\) this gives \(-6\), but the graph shows \(-12\). Multiplying all the heights by 2 preserves the roots.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Why say “equal roots”?}\[x^2-12x+36=(x-6)^2\]The root 6 occurs twice as a factor. There is one distinct root, with multiplicity 2.

\textbf{Fundamental theorem of algebra}\par Every polynomial of degree \(n\ge1\) has exactly \(n\) complex roots when counted with multiplicity.\par The degree is the highest power with a nonzero coefficient. A quadratic has degree 2.\par Thus a quadratic always has two complex roots counting multiplicity, even when it has no real roots.

\textbf{An example of factorisation over the reals}\[\begin{aligned}x^4+a^4&=(x^2+\sqrt2ax+a^2)\\&\quad\times(x^2-\sqrt2ax+a^2)\end{aligned}\]Expanding gives \((x^2+a^2)^2-2a^2x^2=x^4+a^4\).\par Every real polynomial can be factored into real linear and quadratic factors.

transcription.tex: \text{A car manufacturer uses a model to predict the fuel consumption, }y\text{ miles per gallon (mpg), for a specific model of car travelling at a speed of }x\text{ mph.}\quad y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16,\ x>0.\quad\par (a) \text{Use the model to find two speeds at which the car has a fuel consumption of 32.5 mpg.}\par (b) \text{Rewrite }y\text{ in the form }A-B(x-C)^2,\text{ where }A,B,C\text{ are constants to be found.}\par (c) \text{Using your answer to part b, find the speed at which the car has the greatest fuel efficiency.}\par (d) \text{Use the model to calculate the fuel consumption of a car travelling at 120 mph.} \text{Comment on the validity of using this model for very high speeds.}
(c) At \(x=48.75\) mph, the squared term is zero and \(y\) is greatest.
(d) \[y=-0.01(120)^2+0.975(120)+16=-11\]Negative mpg is impossible. The model is not valid at very high speeds.

transcription.tex: \text{A fertiliser company uses a model to determine how the amount of fertiliser used, }f\text{ kilograms per hectare, affects the grain yield }g,\text{ measured in tonnes per hectare.}\quad g=6+0.03f-0.00006f^2.\quad\par (a) \text{According to the model, how much grain would each hectare yield without any fertiliser?}\par (b) \text{One farmer currently uses 20 kilograms of fertiliser per hectare. How much more fertiliser} \text{would he need to use to increase his grain yield by 1 tonne per hectare?}
(a) At \(f=0\), the yield is 6 tonnes per hectare.
(b) \[\begin{aligned}g(20)&=6.576\\6+0.03f-0.00006f^2&=7.576\\f&\approx59.6\text{ or }440.4\end{aligned}\]The smaller increase is \(59.6-20=39.6\) kg per hectare (1 d.p.).

transcription.tex: \text{A football stadium has 25000 seats. The football club know from past experience that they will sell only 10000 tickets if each ticket costs }\pounds30.\text{ They also expect to sell 1000 more tickets every time the price goes down by }\pounds1.\quad\textbf{a}\quad\text{The number of tickets sold }t\text{ can be modelled by the linear equation }t=M-1000p,\text{ where }\pounds p\text{ is the price of each ticket and }M\text{ is a constant. Find the value of }M.\quad\text{(1 mark)}\par (a) Find \(M\).\par \text{The total revenue, }\pounds r,\text{ can be calculated by multiplying the number of tickets sold by the price of each ticket. This can be written as }r=p(M-1000p).\quad\par \textbf{b} \text{Rearrange }r\text{ into the form }A-B(p-C)^2,\text{ where }A,B,C\text{ are constants to be found. (3 marks)}\par \textbf{c} \text{Using your answer to part b or otherwise, work out how much the football club should} \text{charge for each ticket if they want to make the maximum amount of money. (2 marks)}\par (c) Find the price that maximises revenue.
(c) Charge \(\pounds20\), giving revenue \(\pounds400,000\).\par Sales are 20,000 tickets, within the 25,000-seat capacity.

slides.title: Would you like $1,000,000 for finding roots?

transcription.tex: Roots are inputs that give an output of zero. Finding roots can also lead to major research problems.\par For real \(s>1\), the Riemann zeta function can be defined by\[\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^s}\]\[\zeta(2)=1+\frac1{2^2}+\frac1{3^2}+\cdots\]The function extends to complex inputs through a more advanced definition.

\textbf{The Riemann hypothesis}\par It predicts that every nontrivial zero of the extended zeta function has real part \(1/2\).\par This is a Millennium Prize Problem with a US$1 million prize for a qualifying solution. It connects zeros of a function with the distribution of prime numbers.
